watch.text: Centuries ago, Mastro Cherry found an ordinary log in his workshop.
When he raised his hatchet, a child's voice begged him to be careful.
He searched every corner, but no hidden speaker could be found.
The wood cried under a blow and laughed beneath the carpenter's plane.
Then Geppetto arrived, seeking wood for a marvelous traveling marionette.
The mischievous log used a hated nickname and provoked two comic quarrels.
After making peace, Geppetto accepted the strange gift and carried it home.
In his poor room, he named the puppet Pinocchio and began carving.
The unfinished eyes moved, and the nose stretched longer than he planned.
The new puppet mocked Geppetto and stole his yellow cap.
Geppetto taught him to stand as soon as the legs were finished.
Pinocchio learned one step, then raced through the open door.
His wooden feet clattered while Geppetto chased him down the street.
A Carabineer stopped the runaway by grabbing his extremely long nose.
Pinocchio collapsed dramatically, and the crowd blamed his worried father.
The officer released the puppet and led innocent Geppetto to prison.

watch.text: While Geppetto sat in prison, Pinocchio celebrated being completely free.
The century-old Talking Cricket warned him to respect his father.
Pinocchio rejected school, honest work, and every uncomfortable piece of advice.
When the Cricket predicted trouble, the angry puppet threw a hammer.
His victory felt empty as hunger filled the cold, bare house.
The only egg cracked open, and a cheerful chick escaped through the window.
Outside, Pinocchio begged for food but received a bucket of cold water.
He returned soaked and fell asleep with his feet beside the stove.
By morning, both wooden feet had burned completely away.
Geppetto returned from prison and listened to Pinocchio's desperate story.
Though he was hungry too, the old man offered his last three pears.
Pinocchio first refused the skins and cores, then ate them gratefully.
Geppetto agreed to replace the feet only after a sincere promise.
The puppet apologized and declared that he would go to school.
His father carved and attached two sturdy new wooden feet.
Finally, Geppetto sold his only coat to buy the promised primer.

watch.text: Pinocchio started toward school, proudly carrying the primer Geppetto had sacrificed for.
Music from a nearby puppet theater made him forget every promise.
He sold the precious book and spent the money on a ticket.
Onstage, the wooden actors immediately recognized Pinocchio as their long-lost brother.
They abandoned the play and greeted him with noisy affection.
Their enormous director, Fire Eater, entered and demanded an explanation.
He blamed Pinocchio for the ruined performance and threatened to burn him.
The terrified puppet called for his father and begged for mercy.
Fire Eater's repeated sneezes revealed that his anger was beginning to soften.
He spared Pinocchio but ordered Harlequin burned beneath the roasting dinner.
Pinocchio refused to celebrate while his innocent friend faced danger.
He begged, argued, and finally offered to replace Harlequin himself.
The selfish runaway suddenly acted with loyalty and genuine courage.
Fire Eater lifted him up, deeply moved by the sacrifice.
He pardoned Harlequin and decided to eat his dinner uncooked.
The entire puppet company danced with relief until dawn.

watch.text: Fire Eater gave Pinocchio five gold pieces to carry home to Geppetto.
The puppet imagined food, clothing, and a new coat for his father.
On the road, a limping Fox and supposedly blind Cat approached him.
They described a magical field where buried coins would multiply overnight.
A Blackbird exposed the story as a trick and urged Pinocchio home.
The Cat quickly silenced the bird before the warning could sink in.
Pinocchio chose the exciting promise and followed them to the Red Lobster Inn.
His new friends ordered an enormous meal while pretending to be unwell.
Before midnight, they disappeared and left Pinocchio responsible for the bill.
After paying one coin, he continued alone along the dark road.
The ghost of the Talking Cricket offered one final warning to return.
Two masked Assassins appeared and chased Pinocchio deep into the forest.
He hid the remaining four coins beneath his tongue and refused to speak.
After a desperate escape, he raced toward a distant white house.
The Assassins caught him near a giant oak when the door stayed closed.
They left him suspended from a branch while the violent wind rose.

watch.text: The Blue Fairy noticed Pinocchio hanging helplessly from the giant oak.
She sent a Falcon to cut the rope and rescue him.
Her elegant Poodle carried the puppet home in a tiny carriage.
A Crow, Owl, and Talking Cricket debated whether their patient was alive.
Pinocchio refused the bitter medicine until Black Rabbits arrived for him.
He swallowed it immediately and recovered from his dangerous fever.

watch.text: The Fairy prepared a celebration for Pinocchio's transformation into a real boy.
Pinocchio went out to invite Lamp-Wick, his closest and laziest friend.
Lamp-Wick announced that he was leaving for the famous Land of Toys.
He described a country without schools, books, teachers, or any required work.
Pinocchio remembered the Fairy's promise, but endless play sounded irresistible.
At midnight, a crowded wagon arrived to carry the boys away.
The exhausted donkeys pulling it seemed to whisper warnings through their tears.
Pinocchio ignored every sign, squeezed aboard, and abandoned the waiting celebration.
In Toyland, children played from morning until night without correction.
Five carefree months passed without a single lesson or useful task.
Then Pinocchio awoke and discovered long donkey ears on his head.
A Marmot examined him and sadly diagnosed incurable Donkey Fever.
Pinocchio covered the ears and hurried to check on Lamp-Wick.
His friend was hiding the same ears beneath an oversized cap.
Laughter changed into braying as both boys became complete donkeys.
The wagon driver sold Pinocchio to a new owner and collected his profit.

watch.text: A circus owner bought Donkey Pinocchio and trained him through punishment.
Soon the animal performed bows, dances, and dangerous jumps before crowds.
During one bright performance, Pinocchio recognized the Blue Fairy in the audience.
He tried to call her name, but his mouth produced only a donkey's bray.
Confused and distracted, Pinocchio missed a jump and injured one leg.
The circus owner immediately sold the lame donkey for almost nothing.
His next owner cared only about using the skin for a drumhead.
The man tied a heavy stone to Pinocchio and dropped him underwater.
Hungry fish consumed the donkey covering while the protected wooden body remained.
When the rope rose, the surprised buyer found a living marionette instead.
Pinocchio slipped free and explained that the Fairy had protected him.
While he swam away, an azure Goat called from a white rock.
Before he could reach safety, the Terrible Shark appeared nearby.
Its mouth opened like a cave and pulled the swimmer inward.
Pinocchio was swallowed before he could change direction.
In the darkness, a large Tunny explained that escape seemed impossible.

watch.text: Pinocchio left the Tunny and followed a tiny light through the darkness.
At a small table, an old man ate beside his final candle.
The white-haired prisoner was Geppetto, the father Pinocchio had searched for.
They embraced in disbelief, laughing and crying at the same time.
Pinocchio poured out the entire story of his mistakes and misfortunes.
Geppetto explained how the storm and Terrible Shark had swallowed him.
He had survived inside the monster for two long years.
Supplies from a swallowed merchant ship had provided food, candles, and matches.
Now the food was gone, and the candle on the table was the last.
Pinocchio insisted that they attempt an escape before darkness returned.
Although Geppetto could not swim, Pinocchio promised to carry him.
The ancient Shark's asthma forced it to sleep with its mouth open.
Their first attempt failed when a sudden sneeze threw them backward.
Pinocchio refused despair, took his father's hand, and climbed again.
At the final row of teeth, Geppetto climbed onto his son's back.
Pinocchio leaped into the moonlit water and began carrying them home.

watch.text: Pinocchio carried Geppetto through the sea until his strength began failing.
The friendly Tunny arrived and carried both exhausted travelers safely ashore.
On the road, the ruined Fox and Cat begged their former victim for money.
Pinocchio remembered their theft, rejected their excuses, and continued with his father.
The Talking Cricket welcomed them into a small straw cottage.
Pinocchio apologized for the hammer and prepared a bed for Geppetto.
Farmer John offered warm milk in exchange for one hundred buckets of water.
Every morning, Pinocchio completed the hard work to feed his weak father.
At the farm, he discovered Lamp-Wick dying after a donkey's life of exhaustion.
For five months, Pinocchio worked by day and studied by lamplight.
He sold baskets, supported Geppetto, and built him a comfortable rolling chair.
Eventually he saved fifty pennies and planned to buy new clothes.
The Snail then reported that the Blue Fairy was sick and penniless.
Pinocchio gave away every coin and doubled his work for her.
That night, the Fairy praised his loving heart and forgave his past.
He awoke as a real boy in a renewed home beside a healthy Geppetto.
